raw_comment:
1. In America, more than half of people of all ages who responded to this survey work  in person. However, a quarter of people who have bachelor’s degrees or graduate degrees work from home. Even some high school students or those with less education have a home-based job. 
2. I wonder what kinds of jobs some high school students or those with less education do remotely. In my community, most high school students work in person. For instance, they work at convenience stores or supermarkets. So, I can’t imagine what kinds of jobs American high school students have. 
3. If working remotely becomes widespread and popular in my community, it will be difficult for young people to learn manners as a member of society and how to communicate with other people well. 
4. What is Your Working Style?

raw_comment:
Immediately striking is the strong correlation between education level and work flexibility. Workers with a bachelor's degree or higher are much more likely to work hybrid or fully remotely, while workers with a high school diploma or less overwhelmingly work in person. This trend puts into light the effect of education on job type and flexibility.
Moreover, racial and age disparities in hybrid/remote work opportunities reflect broader inequities in job distribution and accessibility.

Why do workers with more education have more remote opportunities? Is this a job-type issue, a technological access issue, or a preference of employers?
How has the pandemic reshaped workforce norms? For example, will the increase in remote work stabilize or continue to grow?

In many communities, including mine, this graph reflects ongoing shifts toward hybrid or remote work in office jobs. Friends and family with college degrees have seen improved work-life balance due to remote options. However, those in service or healthcare roles still have to work in person, often facing long commutes and inflexible schedules. This highlights the need for systemic changes to address these disparities.

Work Flexibility Depends on Education: A New Divide in the Post-Pandemic World.

raw_comment:
What is the first that I noticed about this graph? Well, that would be the amount of red that there was. The red on the graph indicates the number of people who work in person. Each section is separated by the level of education a person has. No matter the amount of education a person has, most of the time, people will work in person. However, I did notice that the more education a person has, the less likely it is to be in person. Now, they are to work for what I wonder. Well, I am not too sure if I am wondering too much about the graph. I do understand that each section is separated by education level, and I understand that with more education, the more "sophisticated" a job gets. This is not the correct wording because it is not to say that a person with only a high school diploma cannot have a sophisticated job. I think this relates to me by really highlighting how my progression of jobs has looked throughout my education. 

My headline: Covid Online

I notice that there are more high school workers in general in this data set and most of them are in person workers. I notice that overall, in person work covers a majority of the data set and then there are the other two categories.

How does this relate to me and my community?
This relates to me because I am about to have a college degree and will be working in person however I know many people still working from home.

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
I noticed that a lot more people that have a degree work online or hybrid than people that have high school or some college. 

What do I wonder? 
I wonder what type of jobs people with degrees have compared to people without degrees and how does it affect in person vs not. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because I know people who are fully online, hybrid, and in-person. Their lives all look very different from one another and it is interesting to see and compare. This also tells me what the future could look like.

Outbreak changed the way we work

I noticed that it is a lot more common for people to work in person than hybrid or completely asynchronous.

I wonder what this graph looked like before the pandemic happened. I feel that working completely remote was not a common thing, so of course suddenly the percentages will go up.

1. **Chart type**: Waffle chart / unit chart with grouped vertical columns.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- The chart uses **grouped columns** by education level along the x-axis.  
- Within each column, colored unit squares are **stacked** to show composition by worker type.  
- No faceting or small multiples.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Education level (High school or less, Some college, Bachelor’s degree, Graduate degree) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped position along x-axis; text labels |
| Number/share of workers | Quantitative | Total height/area of stacked unit squares within each education group |
| Type of worker (In person, Hybrid, Fully remote) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit squares; stacked segments; legend |
raw_comment:
I notice that there are more people working in high school than any other category, but the workers with a at least some college is greater than the ones without.  
I also notice that the portion of hybrid and remote jobs is least for those with high school only or less.  The largest number of workers working hybrid or remote are those with bachelors, but the portion of hybrid or remote workers from the graduate degree category seems to be a greater percentage.  
I wonder about the advantages of having the squares rather than a bar.  This means there isn't a need for a y-axis, I guess.  
My community has a low cost of living. People working remotely can move to our area and experience higher quality of housing with lower costs.  There has been some effort to draw these people in.  
A catchy headline might be "Who's back in the Office? Will remote COVID work environments persist?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The higher, your education, the more flexibility you have.  This is something I want for my children.

What do you wonder?
People with bachelors degree may be younger? Therefore working remotely and maybe being a digital nomad could work well? People with graduate degrees might be older? May  have to work in person more or they may crave stability of the office?

How does this relate to you and your community?
I work in medicine and therefore I have more limited opportunities to work remotely. My partner works in finance and has a lot more flexibility since the pandemic. This contrast between our work obligations became a sore spot for us during the pandemic and still continues to bothers me. Although he mostly works in the office now, his mother has a terminal illness and he and his sibling  are able to travel to stay with her weeks at a time to help out but also continue their employment responsibilities. We live in NYC and a lot of our friends have at least one or both partners in a household, who have the ability to work remotely allowing also a reduction in childcare costs and the ability to travel and work in other places.  If I were to do it again I would not have gone to medical school and I would've considered perhaps clinical research and data sciences related career.

Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

Hybrid work is the sweet spot but true flexibility is the icing on the cake

raw_comment:
In the graph, I notice that as the amount of education a person has increases, the more likely it is for them to be a hybrid or fully remote worker. Individuals with high school diplomas, or less, are mostly in-person workers. While those with bachelor's and graduate degrees have an increased chance of becoming hybrid or fully remote workers. However, there are more hybrid and fully remote workers for a bachelor's degree than a graduate degree, which is likely because most people do not pursue a graduate's degree as it is a significant time commitment. 

I wonder how improvements in technology and artificial intelligence will impact hybrid and fully remote workers. AI technology could either improve their efficiency or take away their jobs.

This relates to my community and I as we are starting to use technology more, especially in school. The school provides us with school computers that we use to complete assignments, and if someone is absent, they can catch up easily. Additionally, students can now learn while being fully remote, offering flexibility to those who need it.

A headline that captures the essence of the graph is: The Role of Education in the Post-Pandemic Workforce.

This relates to me because I am currently in high school and do not have any peers who do school fully online or are hybrid; however, that may change once we graduate and start college according to this graph. 2. I wonder why there were so many people who chose to be online rather than going in person regardless of their degrees disregarding the circumstances of the pandemic.
3. I can relate to this with me and my family because when I was going to school during covid, there were options between being hybrid and remote, and it allowed us to be more flexible with spending time together since we were spending much more time at home.
4. A catchy title for this would be, "How the Pandemic Created the Rise of Remote Students"

raw_comment:
I notice that the pandemic has dramatically changed where people work. The graph shows a significant increase in remote work compared to before the pandemic. Many workers now have the option to work from home, and hybrid work combining remote and office work has become much more common. Office attendance has dropped, but it hasn’t disappeared entirely. It’s also interesting to see how flexible work environments are, with some companies offering remote work permanently while others require a return to the office in some capacity.
I wonder if the shift to remote work will stay as high as it is now or if people will return to offices in large numbers once the pandemic's effects lessen more. Will remote work continue to be a popular choice even if there is a shift back to in-person work? I’m curious if remote work is just a temporary trend or if it will become the "new normal."
This shift to remote and hybrid work is relevant to me and my community because many of us are in school or early in our careers, and the way people work will impact our future job opportunities and daily lives. In my community, more people are working from home or doing hybrid schedules, which means fewer people are commuting to work every day.
A catchy headline would be "Work Anywhere, Anytime: How the Pandemic Changed Where We Work Forever."

raw_comment:
1. The graph shows that people with higher degrees are more likely to have hybrid or fully remote jobs. This makes sense because a lot of those jobs need skills you usually learn in college, and they can often be done online.  

2. Seeing this makes me wonder if more in-person jobs will eventually become remote or hybrid. As online work keeps growing and technology gets better, it seems like even jobs that used to always be in person could start offering remote options.  

3. This really connects to my family because it could make things easier for us. If my parents had more flexible work schedules, they could spend more time at home and wouldn’t have to stress as much about who’s watching my younger siblings.  

4. Title: The Rise of Hybrid and Remote Work.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 

I noticed that each education level got considerably lower after high school. After high school till graduate degree, the amount of people in that education group loses many boxes, or 50,000 people each. In addition, I also noticed that the amount of in-person people grow considerably lower while going to graduate degrees, and values such as hybrid and fully remote grow considerably. I guess we can correlate this to the amount of choice people have as they go to higher levels of education.

What do you wonder?

I wonder what correlation the amount of education you have has on what form of work you will experience in the future. What do you learn differently, or in the job you get that gives you the freedom of choice you have.

How does this relate to you and your community? 

This is related to me and my community because I live in the silicon valley where many companies are situated. The topic of discussion is always different companies offering different working situations to their employees. Some companies allow a hybrid work form while others require employees to come in everyday. By understanding what form of education each employee has in these different companies we can somewhat understand the reason behind these choices. 


Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

The World of Knowledge: How Does The Amount of Education You Have Affect Your Work Form

%3.4 remote

%87.7 in person 
%5.7 hybrid 
%7.6 remote

%17.3 remote

My father has a graduate degree and works hybrid, which seems to be a pretty large amount of workers like him.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

94.3 % of High School Graduates are in-person
3.4% of High School Graduates are fully remote
2.3% of High School Graduates are hybrid

87.7% of people with some college education  are in-person
5.7% of people with some college education are hybrid
7.6% of people with some college education are fully remote

16.1% of people with a Bachelor’s degree are hybrid
17.3% of people with a Bachelor’s degree are fully remote
66.6% of people with a Bachelor's degree are in-person

17.3% of people with a Graduate degree are fully remote
61.2% of people with a Graduate degree are in-person
21.5% of people with a Graduate degree are hybrid

I notice that the higher level of education one has, the more likely they are to work remotely or have a hybrid work setting.
What do you wonder?

I wonder why jobs that are in-person generally don’t need or require a higher level of education such as bachelors or graduate degrees. I also wonder what type of job doesn’t need you to actually be at a work site outside of home.

How does this relate you and your community?

My dad has multiple jobs, and one is hybrid and the other is also hybrid. My dad has a bachelors degree, and works as a civil engineer as well as an architect. Furthermore, I think these statistics show how the people around us and their jobs are affected by their level of education.

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I noticed that most of individuals whom obtained a high school or lower level of education work in person compared to the rest. But as the graph increases in the level of education, more people are employed in virtual jobs.  I wonder if these virtual shifts were already set to occur due our ever-lasting modernizing society or if COVID really influenced the change.  This relates and connects to me and my community, as this greatly effected how me and many others attended school. Not only have I had to work virtually as a student during the pandemic, but we also had to experience the change back to in person. I feel that anything virtual isn't really helpful whether its job wise or educational wise. I found myself sleeping and not working to my best ability during virtual class, and also found myself not connecting with others and just losing a lot of social skills.
A title for this text would be " Life After COVID: Will Jobs Ever Be The Same?"

raw_comment:
I noticed that after the 2020 COVID-19 Pandemic education systems have changed incredibly. For example, after the pandemic students had the option to do remote learning, hybrid learning or in person learning. But prior to the pandemic, students only had the option for in person learning. Along with that, as the level of education changes, the number of in-person learners continues to decrease from high school to a graduate's degree.

I wonder if that the pandemic did not happen, then would we still have the option to do online learning? Would people still rely on technology as much as they do now? I believe that because of the pandemic we have started to rely on technology as much as possible and now it is difficult to imagine a world without it.

This relates to me because my parents work in person jobs however, my aunt works a hybrid job. My parents usually come home around 6:00 pm whereas my aunt is home all day. While its convenient for my cousins to have their mom at home with them all day, I take care of my sister and I until my parents come home from work which helps me and my sister to become independent.

raw_comment: I notice that there is a trend with the amount percentage of people working full time in person decreasing with each level of education. In high school, the percentage of people working in person is greatest while those with a graduate degree of bachelor's degree seem to be the lowest.  This change is likely due to Covid, which introduced the opportunity to work home for many. In most cases, this is more convenient for the worker. I wonder whether or not this change would have occurred without the introduction of Covid. I believe that it would have still occurred, but to a much lesser extent because of growing technology and the greater need for conveniency in our daily lives. This relates to me because my mother works hybrid at her job, and it is much more convenient since she can pick me up from school at whatever time I require. However, if my mother was in the office, it would take around half an hour to pick me up compared to 10 minutes. I assume that this is also similar to guardians who work hybrid which children in school as well. In conclusion, I would name this graph "The ratio of different working environments in tandem with level of education" since that is what the graph most accurately reflects.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that people with a bachelor's or graduate degree work more remote jobs than those with high school or associate's degrees. I also noticed that if you compare all the ratios of remote workers out of the total workers, the graduate degree workers have the highest ratio.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if there are more remote jobs open to people with degrees vs people without degrees. I also wonder what the same graph would look like pre covid? Would there be a large difference in the number of remote workers?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This is relatable to my community because as these ways of working evolve, everyone is affected by them. I know several people who work remotely, and it makes a large difference in their lives.

raw_comment: Headline: Remote Work Revolution is a Mirage.   I notice how small the number of remote workers is as a percentage of working people and I wonder why this group gets such out sized coverage of their situation in the media. of course one answer to this question suggests itself in the graph: the highly "educated" are over represented among remote workers and their lifestyles are generally over-reported.  It's amusing to think that this small group of lucky and privileged people sometimes talk about remote work as if it were a fundamental right that they will never relinquish. This is a strange way to think of a temporary policy implemented during a health crisis that came and went. But, here we are.

But no amount of hard work or enthusiasm for my education got me past the typing test requirement at many interviews in the 80s.  HR algorithms do the same thing now. Luckily I was not a liberal arts major as no stem boot camp was around to give me a skill that would get hired

K

raw_comment:
1. I notice that people in high school (or less) had school more in person rather than remote or hybrid. Adding on to that, those with bachelor’s degrees have been in hybrid and online more than others, but it does not have as much when it comes to in-person learning. However, “some college” has more in-person, but less total than the other two. I also notice how small the graduate degree’s column is.

2. I wonder why the graduate degree’s column is so low; is it supposed to show how less total students have graduate degrees, or is it showing that some people didn’t even show up? I also wonder why so many student in high school or less did in-person learning rather to online regarding the pandemic? 

3. This relates to me because I had gone through the pandemic as an elementary student. It’s fascinating to know that so many more kids had gone to school in person rather than what I did, which was online learning.

4.
Graduates or Youngins: Is 6 Feet Apart More Than Just At Grocery Stores?

raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Why Does Work Get More Remote the Higher Your Education?” by Logan of Juneau, Alaska; "Remote Work Grows with Education" by Mateo of Fla.; "Does Your Level of Education Increase Your Chances of Remote Work?" by Saheed of Lagos; “How Your Education Level May Impact Your Work Style” by Giovana of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Convent Station, N.J.; "Degrees of Separation: How Education Shapes Job Flexibility" by Fernanda of Perth Amboy High School in N.J. and “Can a High Education Lead to Work from One's Bed?” by Aubree of Netherland High School in Tex.

 

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.

1. I notice that as the level of education increases, from early education like high school to a graduate degree so does the amount of people working remotely. Students in high school have more people working in person compared to the others. This could be because high schoolers aren't offered jobs online due to the education level required and have more options in person. For example at fast food restaurants or baby-sitting jobs.

2. I wonder what the statistics would've been like if the pandemic hadn't happened. I wonder if they'd still be similar or drastically different.

3. This is similar to my community as I see majority of high schoolers working in person. People with bachelor's and graduate degrees work more online. However, there is also a large portion of college graduates working hybrid, as I see people in my community working from home on some days and others going in person.  

4. Work from home once you're grown

Looking at the graph it implies that most people in my community work in-person jobs rather than fully remote or a hybrid type.

4. A catchy headline for this graph could be "Here or There, Jobs are Everywhere."

raw_comment:
After looking closely at this graph I instantly notice the domination of pink squares on the graph in every bar no matter the education level. Pink is always dominating. It does make sense though as the majority of jobs are in person. 

Something I wonder is if there is a correlation between education level and the amount of fully remote or hybrid jobs, this idea looks to be true from (some high school) to (bachelors degree) but when it gets to graduate degree workers the correlation seems to stop as the amount of hybrid/fully remote decreases.

This graph seems pretty relatable to me seeing as though people in my family that have a bachelor degree were granted opportunities to work both in person and in a hybrid setting.

A catchy title for this headline could be 
"More Time In School Less Time At The Office"

raw_comment: The graph on the New York Times page represents the types of jobs individuals have worked since the pandemic of 2020. A small detail that is noticeable to the eye is the large amount of "In-Person" workers whose education is in high school or less. Another noticeable attribute is that the higher degrees individuals have in academics, the more likely they are can work hybrid jobs, or fully remote jobs. This could potentially mean that more educated people were less likely to have been affected by the pandemic than others.

raw_comment:
1. From this graph, I noticed that our society relies most heavily on in-person jobs. As the graph progresses in the level of education, more people are involved in virtual jobs.
2. After studying this graph, I wonder if these virtual shifts were bound to take place given our modernizing society or if the pandemic was needed to propel these changes. I also wonder, especially considering the differences in degrees, what this graph would look like if we only considered office jobs or typical 9-5s. I feel that these have been the greatest affected by the virtual shift.
3. This relates to me specifically, as I have worked both ways. Not only have I had to work virtually as a student during the pandemic, but I have also worked virtually for my uncle's law firm. I have numerous jobs throughout the year where I work fully in person, and I have to say I far prefer these. I don't think anything virtual can match the level of human interaction and connection that is built in an in-person workspace.
4. A World Post-Pandemic: Will the Workspace Ever Be the Same?

raw_comment: Looking at this graph, I notice that most people who attend school remotely, whether that be hybrid or fully remote, are working for their bachelor's degree; however, about 40% of people in graduate school are working hybrid or remote which is the largest proportion in each given category. This makes me wonder if the only reason that people receive educations remotely is because of covid or if there are there other reasons. This would be easy to determine by seeing the graph prior to covid. This relates to my community because now more and more people are beginning to work from home instead of in person. A catchy title would be "Working After Covid."

raw_comment:
Online Employees vs Their Education
I notice that overall the majority of workers are in person however there is a percent in each graph where employees work fully remote or hybrid. I also notice a trend of an increase in the percent of people working remote and hybrid jobs as the level of education advances. Furthermore I wonder why this is and I believe I know why. Thinking about the jobs that require these higher levels of education it makes sense that they are able to do more out of office work. Here in southeast Texas a lot of the industry is dominated by refineries and looking at the work structures of these refineries we can see how this trend is proven. Looking at the lower ranks of refineries we have the blue collar hands, most of which only graduated high school, do repairs and maintenance on the equipment use and that require the employees to be there on site. However for someone higher up like an engineer, all of which have  level of education past high school,  occasionally go out into the field but most of the time are in their offices doing calculations, looking at numbers, or in meetings all of which can be done on a computer.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that most people out of all 4 groups of degrees were working in-person. There wasn't much of a difference between the number of people working hybrid or the number of people who were fully remote. They are about the same, but don't even compare to the number of in-person workers. I also notice that the better the degree, the more people who could work flexibly. 

2. I wonder how the pandemic affected people economically. Was it harder to earn money remotely versus being in person? I remember how bad the economy was during the pandemic so it makes me wonder about the economic issues at that time.

3. Our community has a lot of refineries and a lot of people had to work in person to make those function. I remember the prices of a lot of products like gas increasing astronomically and it was harder to afford things. This effect is seen even today in certain industries. 

The Degree of Settings

raw_comment:
Headline: How Does the Level of Education Affect the Workplace?
I notice that in-person work remains the most popular option regardless of education. I also noticed that people with less education are more likely to be in-person workers rather than people with a higher level of education. I also noticed that there are significantly fewer people with graduate degrees than at other levels of education. I wonder if higher-educated people are more likely to work hybrid or at home. I also wonder what this information would look like from a previous year. Especially during COVID, I am interested in how the graph would look. I think this graph is trying to display how much time has progressed since COVID-19, when everything was practically online. Now, a majority of people work in person. I also think the graph is trying to display how people with higher education have more opportunities to work either hybrid or from home rather than people with a lower education level. I think this is because people with a higher level of education often have jobs that can be done online. Most jobs for people with a lower level of education are hands-on jobs that you must be in person to attend. This relates to me and my community because there are examples of this within my family. My dad has a graduate degree and works partly from home (hybrid). However, I have not graduated high school, and my job is in-person and cannot be done online.

1.      Most people tend to work in person more for the satisfaction of speaking to others, put there knowledge into something useful and helpful; and getting help from others who have more knowledge, vs sitting on the screen and taking the easy route and simply using "google".

2.      It makes me wonder why some people choose to work at home, People out there tend to be lazy and work at home to eliminate the time of: looking dressed, and socializing with people, they even have easy access to the internet to fill in the boredom of working. 3.      I mean we all have laptops, we all use them to get our work done and do task that are need to improve our grade, but it does get boring looking at a screen and seeing words type out just to delete some from a mistake you have made; I am sure there are certain people who choose to do online, and there is nothing wrong with that, more free time for them I could guess.

4.      " The eyes of those who work", I choose that headline to emphasize that everybody works differently, think of the eyes of someone working at home, the eyes of someone working in person, and the eyes of someone doing both; to me that would be pretty interesting to me seeing how they live life and gain money..

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
I noticed that the percentage of people with remote or hybrid jobs increases with the higher degree. Roughly 5-10% of people with a high school or less education get to work remotely or a mix of in-person and remote jobs. People with Graduate degrees, however, have a 40-50% remote/hybrid to in-person ratio. I believe that the higher level of education a person gets, the more flexible their schedule can be.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why the percentage of people with some college experience have more remote or hybrid jobs despite having no extra qualifications is more than the high school or less category. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community by showing the importance of education to have more preference in my life. It also shows how my community values education.

raw_comment: When analyzing the graph, I noticed that a majority of people, no matter their education, work in person. The graph illustrates that individuals with an education of a high school degree or lower and who have gone to some college are more likely to have a job where that requires in-person work. Additionally, this graph shows that even with a variety of degrees, people can still have jobs that are in-person, hybrid, or fully remote.  One thing I wonder is why one's educational level has an impact on the type of work one will have. The information from the graph relates to my community, specifically my parents. However, my mom's job allows her to be a hybrid. Personally, my mom likes hybrid more than fully remote because, during COVID, she was sick of being home. raw_comment:
1.) I notice that the vast majority of people still attend in person rather than hybrid or fully remote. The number of in person students shrink in college compared to high school but it is still the majority option for all of the options.
2.) I wonder what these numbers looked like before during Covid-19. For a good few months to a year, most everyone attended school online. I wonder what those numbers looked like and would love to see the timeline of people gradually changing back to in person.
3.) This relates to me and my community because our community is mainly based on in person jobs. Very few jobs in my community allow for hybrid or remote working. Jobs such as the refineries, medical field, and teaching are prominent jobs in my community that require you to work in person.
4.) A catchy headline that captures this graph's main idea could be, "Couch or Cubicle? How Covid-19 Shaped the Way we Work."

raw_comment:
I noticed that many people work in person. People who have a high school or less education are more likely to work in person than someone who has a bachelor’s or graduate degree. I noticed that several fully remote people are likelier to have obtained a bachelor’s degree than someone with a high school or less degree. 

I wonder if a high degree correlates to the time spent working in person versus at home. I wonder if the stats have changed in 2024. I wonder how remote working impacts the specific industry and whether it is impacted negatively or positively. I wonder how this will change in the future. 

This relates to my community because my mom works from home, allowing her to be there for me and my milestones, like sports, while earning a living. This also relates to my community because my generation has been through middle and high school, affecting how we see at-home working versus in-person working. Growing up near a big city where there is the option to have in-person versus remote work allows me to experience what it is like to live two different lives at the same time

raw_comment:
I noticed that in all the levels of education, majority of people are in person workers. I've also noticed that in the higher education levels, like Bachelor's and Graduates, workers are mostly Fully remote or Hybrid which means that the higher the education level, the more chances you have to work in those fields.
I wonder if the workers who are In person feel obligated to work in person because of the requirements that are established in the job, or are just choosing to go in person.
This is related to me and the community because it is showing us the rates of the types of workers in my community and area, and in other communities who are in the work field. It also provides insights of what most jobs need in order to work in that certain field.

Something that I noticed is the vast majority of people have in-person jobs rather than online or hybrid jobs. 
 Since the pandemic widely affected the United States,  I wonder what makes the number of in-person jobs higher than the online jobs. I question this because after the pandemic many companies and businesses were still shut down and the online jobs was what everyone had to do because of quarantine.  In Nederland, Texas there are a whole lot of jobs that are in-person jobs. For example this part of Texas is known for the refineries and oil companies. raw_comment:

What I wonder: What type of hybrid and remote jobs are offered to those in high school and/or lower education? I also wonder if the pandemic created more online job opportunities. 
This relates to me because I am a high schooler looking for a job, but my schedule often conflicts with most of the jobs I have looked at. Instead of finding a job in person, I could find a remote or hybrid job that works around my schedule.  
Headline: How the Pandemic Changed the Workforce

I also notice that it appears that around 50% or 40% of those with a graduate degree are either working hybrid, or fully remote, which could indicate that a higher education results in more flexibility to work at home or in person.

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
A person with a bachelor's degree is most likely out of all the degrees to work fully remote or in a hybrid setting. This could pertain to those holding graduate degrees being involved in higher education, research, or teaching. Additionally, those in the workforce with a high school or college degree are more likely to work jobs requiring being in person such as working at a store, construction, or maintenance work.
What do I wonder?
Does the high percentage of high-degree earners working remotely or in hybrid settings impact the productivity of their work? If so how will this impact our society as a whole? Additionally, in what way does this cause disconnect and disorganization between workers, bosses, and clientele?
How does this affect my community?
This affects my community because it shows us that although a degree could change your chances of working hybrid or virtually, many people no matter the degree they earned are working in person post-COVID. Thus, creating a connection between many people regardless of the level of education they received.
Create a catchy title for this graph.
Checked Out: Are people still working from home or is it purely a mental state?

raw_comment:
I notice that majority of all types of people work in person. But, the higher the level of education there is, more people are working hybrid or fully remote. I also noticed that well over most people in high school are in person. I wonder why most people that work fully remote are one's with their Bachelor's degree, and why there are very few people with their graduate degree who work in person. In addition, I also wonder what this graph would look like if the COVID pandemic never occurred. I wonder if most people would just be working in person full time. This relates to me and my community because back during COVID, I had to join school fully virtual for a few months, then I went hybrid and fully in person. Most people that were in school and working during the pandemic had to experience the different types of learning (virtual,hybrid,in person).

raw_comment:
Headline : Will your education allow you to work in person or at home? 
This graph shows where people are working based on the level of education they have. I notice there are three type of work options, in person, hybrid, and full remote. I also notice that the people that have a high school education or less tend to work in person more than people with a college education or higher. As the level of education increases the more common it is to work in a remote environment. This makes me wonder if the level of education received affects the work environment someone ends up in. I wonder if the jobs that require a high school education or less are labor jobs. Labor jobs require for people to work in person. This relates to me and my community because I want to further my education and receive a high degree.

raw_comment:
Zooming through Zoom.

1. What I notice is remote work had a big change on people with graduates and bachelors degree but colleges and high school employees are little to no change at all. It could be like this because high school and college jobs are more likely to be working at fast food places or in person jobs, where the people who have degrees are more into “real world” jobs where meetings take place on zoom, emails and projects are all on software. 
2. I wonder if remote work will continue rather than die out, as people are used to the online workflow because of the 2020-2022 full scale zoom work life. 
3. This relates to me and my community because as a whole, every single being was affected by the pandemic in there work life.

raw_comment:
What do I notice? 

I notice that as people get older they most likely have more responsibilities such as paying rent, taking care of family, or other things that come with getting older. Due to this they most likely have to get a job or spend more time off campus to keep up with their daily lifestyle. 

What do I wonder?  

I wonder how this might affect their grades or their overall participation with the class. Some effects of bad grades could be stress from outside school life, not fully focused during lectures, or having no time during the day to devote to class. 

How does this affect my community? 

This could effect the community since their will be less people traveling through areas of where their job is located. This can lead to an economic decline for smaller companies, gas stations, and potentially restaurants as well. 

Create a catchy title for this graph: 

From offices to zoom, how Covid-19 still effects our daily lives.

What do I notice? The graph shows the type of work (in-person, hybrid, or remote) for different education levels. Most people with lower education, like high school or some college, work in-person. People with higher education tend to work more remotely or in hybrid jobs.

What do I wonder? I wonder why those with higher education work more remotely. Are there enough remote jobs for people with lowered education? Also, how has the pandemic influenced these trends
How does this relate to you and your community? This is relevant to me and my community because, after the pandemic, many people I know, including my parents, switched to hybrid work. It's interesting to see how their education plays a role in this shift.

Whats going on in this graph? People with higher education are more likely to have jobs that let them work from home, while those with less education mostly work in-person.

This graph displays where people work based on their degree. I notice that there are three types of work options, in-person, hybrid, and online. I also recognize that the people who have a high school degree or less, work in person more than any other degree. Are the jobs that require people to go in possibly labor because labor jobs do not require for people to have a college degree? This relates to my community because as someone who wants to get a college degree, that degree could possibly determine if I work in person, hybrid, or online.

raw_comment:
Headline: Is a good education really a need?
I noticed that there are many workers who have only went to high school or less. In fact, there are staggering amounts of less educated workers compared to workers who have had been to college. Seeing this makes me wonder why there are so little amounts of workers that have a graduates degree. This could relate to my community because I've always believed that one could only have a good job with a stable income if they had been to college and gotten a degree, but this could prove that it isn't needed. It also connects to my community because there are definitely many of those who haven't been to college, but provide for their family successfully still.

1. This graph shows how people worked in 2023. I noticed that a larger percentage of those with a Bachelor's or Graduate degree worked remotely or hybridically than those without degrees. This may be because those with lower education tend to work jobs that require manual labor, which can not be attended to virtually. It is surprising that the majority of workers only have a high school education or less. I noticed that this graph only includes workers aged 18 to 64, which may have affected the results. 
2. I wonder how these stats have changed from 2020. What types of jobs are most common for each education level? Does virtual working affect job performance? 
3. This relates to me because one of my parents is a hybrid worker.
4. Working Virtually or Virtually Working: How People Work in 2023

raw_comment:
Does one's qualifications truly matter?
Firstly, I noticed that there is an overpowering amount of people with a high school degree or less who work in person. I feel that for the most part this is caused by their academic background. There is also a solid content of people with a college degree who work in person. However, from a high school degree the amount of remote and hybrid workers increases. As we go to the bachelor's degree, we find that this category has the most hybrid and fully remote workers out of any category. Lastly, a graduate's degree almost has a balance. You can categorize hybrid workers and fully remote workers as one group and when you compare them to the in person workers they have a similar amount.
This makes me wonder if it is truly worth it to get a level of education above a bachelor's degree. The graph shows that there are more workers that have obtained a bachelor's degree than those who received a higher education. 
Within my community, I believe that most people have a background that contains a college degree of some sort. Other than a majority of high school students, I feel that mostly everyone works somewhere.

raw_comment:
Headline: From Classroom to Couch: How Education Affects Work Styles
What do I notice? The graph shows the type of work (in-person, hybrid, or remote) for different education levels. Most people with lower education, like high school or some college, work in-person. People with higher education tend to work more remotely or in hybrid jobs.
What do I wonder? I wonder why those with higher education work more remotely. Are there enough remote jobs for people with lower education? Also, how has the pandemic influenced these trends?
What do I think is going on in this graph? People with higher education are more likely to have jobs that let them work from home, while those with less education mostly work in-person.
How does this relate to you and your community? This is relevant to me and my community because, after the pandemic, many people I know, including my parents, switched to hybrid work. It's interesting to see how their education plays a role in this shift.

raw_comment:
In this graph I noticed that people with a more advanced education are more likely to work from home. This makes me wonder why they choose to work from home instead of outside of home since they're more educated. I think if it took me several years to get an education I would want to work in person. However, I can see why they chose remote or hybrid. Maybe they're thinking opposite of me: since it took them so long they should have the ability to work in the comfort of their home. This relates to me and my community because a lot of my friends and I want to go to college and get high educations but all of us want to be hands-on with our job. 

Catchy headline: "Does Your Education Directly Impact the Type of Worker You Are?"

raw_comment:
Headline: "How Covid 19 Changed The Working Environment"
I notice that younger people tend to work in person while some older people work from home. I also notice that people with a graduate degree are more widespread (about half work in person while the other half is either hybrid or fully remote). I wonder why some people still choose to work from home and what jobs offer that option. How are the demographics going to change within the next five years? Will there be more at home workers than in person workers? This relates to me and my community because there could be more online job opportunities once I'm done with school. Whenever the pandemic hit I had to do school virtually and I know a lot of people didn't like it because it was hard.  While working from home seems like a good idea it can be a struggle because you hardly get to interact with people other than your family.

raw_comment:
Headline: "How Covid 19 Changed The Working Environment"
I notice that younger people tend to work in person while some older people work from home. I also notice that people with a graduate degree are more widespread (about half work in person while the other half is either hybrid or fully remote). I wonder why some people still choose to work from home and what jobs offer that option. How are the demographics going to change within the next five years? Will there be more at home workers than in person workers? This relates to me and my community because there could be more online job opportunities once I'm done with school. Whenever the pandemic hit I had to do school virtually and I know a lot of people didn't like it because it was hard.  While working from home seems like a good idea it can be a struggle because you hardly get to interact with people other than your family.

raw_comment: Headline: Remote Work Revolution is a Mirage.   I notice how small the number of remote workers is as a percentage of working people and I wonder why this group gets such outsized coverage of their situation in the media. of course one answer to this question suggests itself in the graph: the highly "educated" are overrepresented among remote workers and their lifestyles are generally overreported.  It's amusing to think that this small group of lucky and privileged people sometimes talk about remote work as if it were a fundamental right that they will never relinquish. This is a strange way to think of a ttemporary policy implemented during a health crisis that came and went. But, here we are.

Headline: Going out or Staying In- the impacts of Covid-19 regarding jobs.
1. I notice that many more people with only a high school degree or less are working in person. As well as I notice their are much less people with a graduate degree than anything else. Since Covid-19 the graph shows the majority of people are back in-person working as represented by the red. 
2. I wonder why more people with high school or less education are in person compared to the other two categories. As well as I wonder how did the pandemic change changed the opportunity for people to work from home.
3.This relates to my community because many of our families were also affected by the pandemic regarding jobs. Most people in my community are working in-person. Although their is that few that got to stay and work from home.

raw_comment:
Headline: How Your Education Level May Impact Your Work Style 

After looking at the graph, I noticed that the number of people working in person decreased as the education level got higher. However, in-person is still the most popular type of work. The largest number of people working in person are those with a high school education or less. I also noticed that hybrid workers are more common compared to fully remote workers for people with a Bachelor's or Graduate degree. I wonder why people with higher education have a bigger opportunity for remote work. And then again, I wonder what types of jobs give more access to remote working and how one makes the decision to start working from home. This graph relates to my community and me because in the future after I attend college, at-home work will probably be 10x more popular compared to in-person.

raw_comment:
Headline: From Classroom to Couch: How Education Shapes Work Styles
What do I notice? 
The graph shows the type of work (in-person, hybrid, or fully remote) for different education levels.
I notice that most people with lower education such as high school or some college work in-person.
On the other hand, people with higher education have more remote and hybrid work.
What do I wonder?
I wonder why people with higher education have more remote work. I wonder if there many jobs available for less educated people to have the luxury of working at home? Also, how has the pandemic changed these work trends?
What do I think is going on in this graph?
People with higher education are more likely to have jobs that allow them to work from home, while those with less education mostly work in-person.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because after the pandemic, my parents and many people I know started to work more hybrid. It's interesting to see that because of their education, they also get that ability to do so.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of 18-64 year olds, regardless of the level of their education, work in person.  I also noticed in the Graduate degree data, there is a more even ratio between working in person, hybrid, or fully remote.  There are also the most hybrid workers within the workers who have received a Bachelor's degree.  I wonder if the in-person workers will increase since the major effects of the pandemic in the workplace have been lessening and people have gone back to work in person.  I also wonder if the hybrid and fully remote methods of working will become an easier option for those who have received education from high school or less and some college since remote work was so common during the pandemic.  This relates to me and my community because I learned remotely from school and both of my parents worked from home and hybrid during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

raw_comment: I noticed that people with less education have gone back to in person work at higher rates than people with higher education. People with a higher education tend to work more fully remote than people with less education. This may be because jobs that come from higher education are most likely easier to complete at home. I also noticed this gray was based on a census from 2023, so the amounts of people at each education level and type of working environment may have changed. I wonder if this graph is an accurate representation of the working population right now. Are there really that many more people with high school education than those with some college? I wonder how this graph found out how many people work in each way it get a representation of all the people in the country that are working age. This relates to my community because it affects the traffic each morning on my way to school because if more people are going to work than there will be more cars on the road causing more traffic. If more people are working remotely than there will be less cars on the road and I will be able to get to school quicker. If I can figure out the patterns of when the hybrid workers go into work and the modes of other peoples jobs it will be easier to determine when to leave. My headline for this would be: Do people really go to the office for work anymore?

raw_comment:
1. I've noticed that individuals with higher education levels often choose to work in hybrid or fully remote arrangements, likely because their fields support such flexibility. I also observed differences in the distribution of education levels among workers. 
It surprised me how few graduate degree holders there are compared to those without college degrees or high school dropouts. This is particularly striking given that earning a graduate degree typically requires just 18-24 months.

2. I wonder how these trends might differ if the pandemic hadn't occurred. Reflecting on this, I think there would likely be fewer hybrid and fully remote workers, as Covid-19 normalized the idea of working from home for many.

3. This trend somewhat connects to our local community, as certain job sectors here could accommodate remote work. However, industries like chemical plants and oil refineries, prevalent in the area, require employees to be physically present at the site.

4. "The Impact of Covid-19 on the Nation's Working Class"

raw_comment:
Headline: "Workplace Shifts Post-Pandemic: In-Person Dominates, but Remote Remains"

What I notice from the graph is that, as we navigate the effects of the pandemic, most people are back working in person post-pandemic, with a few opting for hybrid or remote work. However, remote and hybrid work has grown, particularly among those with higher education levels. College graduates, those with bachelor’s degrees, and even more so graduate degree holders, are working remotely or in hybrid roles at higher rates than those with less education. However, overall, in-person work remains the most popular choice, regardless of education level. I wonder how much of this shift in work patterns will be sustained, and whether younger generations or those in specific fields will continue to prefer remote work in the long run. This graph relates to me and my community, as it highlights a larger societal change that many of us have experienced—navigating the new norms of working from home or in a hybrid model and overall adjusting to pandemic after-effects.

raw_comment:
This graph shows where people work depending on what point of education they are at. I noticed that for all four groups, most of those people work in person. Another thing that stuck out to me was that as education grows, the amount of people working hybrid/remote grows. I wonder why the opportunity for working online grows as your education does. I also wonder if this will be the case a couple of years from now as technology develops and is integrated into more fields. This has a major impact on my life because, as a high school student, I must understand the types of job opportunities available to me! It also applies to my community because in my life a majority of people that I know work remotely or hybrid so I have not interacted with a lot of people who are working fully in person.

raw_comment:
This graph displays where people with different levels of schooling work. In-person work is the most common for every degree; however, being hybrid or fully remote is increasingly common in someone with a Bachelor's degree or Graduate degree. Being in-person for work is the unrivaled most common in someone with a high school degree or less. I wonder if the percentages of hybrid and remote-learning individuals dramatically increased since the pandemic. This relates to me because it is interesting to see my chances of possibly working remote or hybrid in my future career. I currently have less than a high school degree, so it makes sense that I have an in-person job. 
Headline: The Pandemic in the Workforce

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  Today’s graph is about where Americans work since the pandemic – in person (on site), fully remote or hybrid (a combination of both). 2) What do you wonder? - why do people with bachelor's degrees have more of a spread within the three types of workers than the other three categories? Why do people with graduate degrees have fewer hybrid and remote workers than those with bachelor's degrees?

3) How does this relate to you and your community?- Most people I know don't have remote or even hybrid jobs they are always working in person, and mostly they only have a high school diploma education so using the graph it sorta makes sense why that is.

4) What’s going on in this graph?- “From Cubicles to Coffee Shops: The Rise of Flexible Workspaces.”

raw_comment:
What do you notice? I notice that working in-person is more common for all of the given charts.  Hybrid and remote are nearly equal, but still not over-passing in person.  

What do you wonder? Why is it that the education level affects jobs and their flexibility so much? We see that the people with a Graduates degree, AKA the people with the most advanced education level, work less in person. Is it because they have a higher social status or rank, that they tend to work remotely more often?

How does this relate to you and your community?  It overall relates to a lot of highschool students, including myself. Reaching and focusing on a higher education tends to be extremely exhausting and seen as impossible if you’re not “eligible”, or as some would call it, wealthy by generation. As someone that lives in a remote Urban city/town, when the pandemic took place in 2020, everyone was almost forced to risk their health and lives just to earn a couple bucks during the harsh times and inflation. On the other hand, those with a higher education level that are known as “Wealthy” had the choice to either work from home or willingly leave the safety of their homes. In the future, will workplaces be stricter with location?

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I noticed that all people with only a High school diploma go to work in person. Compared to the rest of the people who work remotely the one that has the most amount of people who work remotely is the one who has a bachelor’s degree. I noticed that there not a lot of people go do hybrid compared to those who decided to go in-person.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder if those who went back to in-person and who have only a high school diploma didn’t have a choice of going hybrid. I also wonder if those who work fully remotely do it to be with their families instead of being at work for 8 hours. Did those who go hybrid choose these to spend time with their kids or did they not have a choice?

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
It relates to me and my community because most of the workers here didn’t exactly have a choice to go hybrid or fully remote. The only time that workers had a choice was when we were trying to go back to normal after COVID-19. 

4. Catchy Headline
“From Office Cubicles to Home Desks: The New Normal Workspaces”

I notice that there has been a shift from conventional modes of learning after the COVID19 pandemic. For example, prior to this occurrence, the only method of receiving an education was through in-person learning. However, COVID allowed for the expansion of different modes, including hybrid and online. 

I wonder if it affected the quality of work was damaged due to the transition from fully in-person to online or hybrid. This is an important question because it was unfamiliar to us four years ago, so it may still be difficult to adjust to.

This relates to me and my community because I experienced this transition head-on at the age of 12/13. This shift in how I had to learn was difficult to transition to since there were internet complications at times.

raw_comment:
1. I notice an association between each type of worker in each of the different education levels. A more significant percentage of students who earned a high school degree or less learned in person than people who earned some college degree, bachelor's degree, or graduate degree. More students with a bachelor's degree were fully remote than students with a high school degree or less, bachelor's degree, or graduate degree. A more significant percentage of students who earned a bachelor's degree went on hybrid learning than students who received a high school degree or less, a bachelor's degree, or a graduate degree.

2. I wonder why the variable on the vertical axis was based on the number of workers between the ages of 18 and 64 instead of using a percentage for each category. Would using the number of workers for each category be more precise than using a percentage? I wonder if people who received more than one degree were counted in more than one area or only for the highest or most recent degree.

3. As of 2023, most students, including me, who received less than a high school degree, learned in person. The four types of degrees also display that most workers went in person.

raw_comment:
- I notice that the amount of students that work remotely increases as the education level increases. In turn, the amount of red bars (in-person work) decreases as education level increases. For students getting their bachelor's degree and graduate degree, the amount of people working hybrid and working fully remote is nearly equal while high school and college students tend to be fully remote over hybrid working. 
- I wonder if the number of people who started working remotely has changed after quarantine ended. I know COVID caused many students and adults to experience hybrid and remote work, but have companies transitioned to remote work even after the end of the pandemic?
- As a high school student, this relates to me because while I may work fully in person right now, as I move through education, I may find myself working hybrid or remote. Additionally, during the pandemic, my community and I experienced hybrid and remote work. 
- "The Effect of Education on Remote Work"

raw_comment: This graph displays the types of current workplaces and how different levels of education require different workplaces. I noticed how education of high school or less has more in person than those with bachelor degrees because they are probably working in service level jobs (groercey store workers, etc.) that need to be in person. In contrast, those with bachelor's degrees can probably work from home more since those jobs are more corporate types of jobs. Along with this, I noticed that people with degrees have more of an option to work hybrid or at home because those jobs are typically on computers and devices that do not require face-to-face meetings. I wonder why those with bachelor degrees are fully remote more than those with graduate degrees. I would have thought that they would be similar. This relates to my community and myself because I see the variety of different work profiles between those that work fully remote, hybrid, or only in-person. A headline can be: “Post-Pandemic work environments.”

raw_comment:
Key takeaway: Higher education is correlated with remote.  Somewhat because manual labor requires onsite work, but businesses have kept remote work due to increased cost savings and productivity.
But have there been other impacts?  An increased sense of isolation?  An increased divide between the blue and white collar workers that used to interact at businesses?  Young people losing opportunities to build work relationships? This analysis needs measures such as productivity, mental health, and time.  Nonetheless, this chart will drift to more in-person as companies require days in office, but we will never go back fully.  This new found work-life balance is recognized by even the most hardened CEO.  However, you can’t underestimate the impact of an office.  Interacting in-person connects us and can spark a conversation about a new offering. 
Businesses will always do what is best for the business, and determine the optimal mix.  The ability to find the best person for a job anywhere in the world and selling and delivering services without T&E have positive impacts.  Employees have some leverage in seeking hybrid roles, but that “benefit” is determined by the work force as a whole.  
The intangible impact of in-person and the benefits of remote work must be balanced and both businesses and employees will benefit equally.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the in-person workforce is dominated by people with only a high school diploma. Then the majority of stay-at-home workers are people with bachelor's degrees.

I wonder if going to college will offer more jobs that are accessible from home. Also, why don't people with graduate degrees decide to work from home as much as people with their bachelor's? Is it because people with graduates are in more demand in person? 

Even though both of my parents have their bachelor's in education, they both work in person. But when the pandemic hit my mom became a full-time virtual teacher for a year so she was able to stay at home full-time.

Does your level of education decide where you work? Analyzing how different education experiences disperse the workforce.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the pandemic caused many people to start working from home. The pandemic forced some people out of their in-person jobs and into a less risky environment in their homes. 
  I wonder why we haven't fully gotten back to how society was before the pandemic. People aren't scared to get sick like they were, but we remain isolated in our homes. 
  I see this in my community when I see an ad for DoorDash, online stores, or online tax offices. I can remember when my grandma used to take me and my sister to H-E-B. My grandma hasn't gone into H-E-B in years because she can get her groceries brought out to her car. Simple things like grocery shopping are forever changed. 
  A catchy headline to capture the ideas of this graph is "Post-Pandemic Society".

raw_comment:
What education gets what jobs?
Things I noticed:
1) People with bachelor's degrees are (by a small percentage) more likely to work from home.

2) people who got a high education or less got only in-person jobs

3) There are only a few graduate degrees gotten.

Things I wonder:
What did these statistics look like before covid?

Is the number of people with graduate degrees less due to monetary issues, work incentive issues, or just being unnecessary?
Why do so many people stop at just a high school education?

This graph relates to me and my community by showing how many people have to work in what kind of jobs so we can be a little more informed about what we should set our goals to get the type of jobs we want

I notice that in-person working is the most common method. Most fully remote people have a bachelor's degree. I also saw that the majority of workers have little education. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why in-person is the most common and preferred method. I also wonder if the Covid outbreak increased the amount of remote or hybrid workers. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, it’s clear how much technology has changed the way we work since the COVID-19 pandemic. It allowed people to get things done without actually being at their jobs or schools. Students, teachers, and workers started relying on the internet to finish assignments and tasks remotely. But it makes me wonder—if the pandemic had never happened, would we still be this advanced? Maybe we wouldn’t have the same technological growth or new job opportunities we see now.

This graph really hits home for me and my community because technology is such a big part of how we learn and work. At school, we use assigned computers for classwork, and at home, we’re on Microsoft Teams finishing homework or studying. If COVID-19 hadn’t happened, I feel like we’d still be doing everything on paper—honestly, that sounds like going back to the Dark Ages.

Catchy Headline: How the Pandemic Pushed Us Forward

2. I wonder why people with "graduates degree" have the smallest bar on the graph and a more even amount of the type of workers they have than "some college" or "high school and less" have. Is it because there are less people who actually get a graduate degree?

4. "COVID-19's affect on the working class."

raw_comment: After looking closely at the graph, I noticed that technology vastly improved our ways of working after experiencing the pandemic of COVID-19, as it allowed for work to be done without actually being present at the job. This allowed students, teachers, and various workers to be able to access the internet in order to finish assignments and tasks instead of having to be at your workplace in order to complete it. On the other hand, I wonder what it would have been like if the pandemic had never occurred. We may not be as advanced as we are today with technology and new job opportunities. This graph relates to myself and my community as we use technology such as our assigned computers to complete our daily schoolwork. Even when we go home after school, we continue to work on our computers and Google Classroom to finish our homework and study. If COVID-19 had never happened, we would most likely go back to having most of our assignments and exams on paper, which, in my opinion, is like going back to the Dark Ages. Catchy Headline: Positivity in Pandemic

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the amount of people with high school education have significantly larger numbers of in person workers. In general, the number of in person workers declines as the level of education rises. It also seems to me that with the introduction of online/remote learning from the pandemic, many people stuck with that method and continued to work through technology. I also notice that there is a much less amount of people with higher degrees, such as a graduate degree.
2. This makes me wonder exactly how many people didn't use online methods prior to the pandemic and how many of those people were fond of it enough to continue working through such means. I also wonder why not as many people chose to not further their education after high school.
3. In means of my community, many small businesses and locally owned places were forced to work remotely in efforts to keep their business alive despite their financial state during Covid.
4. Catchy Title: Post Pandemic: The Effects of Different Educational Backgrounds.

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is the amount of in person workers there are for people who have a high school or less education. I also notice there are way more people with jobs that have a high school or less education. This could be because there are more people who don't go to college and they fill the jobs that are in primarily in person. I wonder why people with a bachelor's degree tend to have more jobs that are hybrid or at home out of all the categories. I don't think it relates to our community as much because most of the jobs in our area are in person or a hybrid, but it still requires you to be on the job at some point. With all our refineries and less opportunities with online businesses, I feel like the general population for our area have jobs that are in person or hybrid instead of online.
"Effect on Jobs After Pandemic"

raw_comment:
1. The biggest thing that I noticed is the amount of workers in America who have only received their high school diplomas or might have not finished school at all. The amount of workers that have at the most only high school education severely outweigh the amount of workers in America that received some college education or higher.                                2.  I wonder how exactly the work industry was affected by the whole world shutting down due to the pandemic from a worker's point of view. I also wonder out of all of the jobs that had to turn remote out of their own control, how many companies benefited or were deeply affected by it.  
3.  This graph is very accurate to my community. The majority of the reason people come to work in my community is to work in the refineries, and that cannot be turned into remote work. Not a lot of remote work is still around in the community, after around 2022, everyone returned to their normal life like it was before COVID.
4. How COVID-19 still has a grasp on the world.

raw_comment:
1. I have noticed that since the pandemic has ended most people have gone back to working in person. High school students tend to work in person the most, people with their bachelor's degree have a wider variety of workers, and graduates are the most diverse while also having the least amount of workers.
2. After analyzing this graph, I wonder why there are more high school students working than adults with their graduate degrees.
3. This graph relates to my community because I know many people who never got back to work in person, and if they did there were still many changes. For example, my dad works remotely from home by using his computer and phone. He occasionally had that option in the past, but would still often travel to his office building before the pandemic occurred. 
4. Headline: Does the Impact of Covid-19 Still Affect Workers Today?

raw_comment:
I notice that the 'bachelors degree' has the most amount of fully remote and hybrid workers while 'some collage' has a similar amount of people as 'bachelors degree' but a lot less fully remote and hybrid. 'Graduate degree' has the second most amount fully remote and hybrid workers but has the least amount of people overall. While 'high school or less' has the most amount of people and the least amount of fully remote and hybrid. I also notice that in all of the diagrams in person is the top way they work in each and hybrid being the least. 

I wonder why hybrid is the least and no fully remote. I figured that hybrid would be the second most because a lot of work places include work you have to do by hand. 

As someone in school It makes me think about those around me and how they attend their work.

"Has the way you attend work been effected by the pandemic?"

I notice that the better degree the less people work in person. I also notice that in high school or less almost everyone works in person. I also notice that overall very few people work on line or hybrid. The majority of people work in person. I wonder why most people work in person. I also wonder why the better the degree you get the more chance you have of working online and what types of jobs you can work for remotely and hybrid. How Covid Affected The Working Class

raw_comment:

What interests me is the fact that the people who have bachelor's degrees have the most people working fully remote and/or hybrid. Headliner: "COVID 19's Effects on the Way We Work Now."

raw_comment:
Peoples Education Through Degrees
When looking at the graph you can see that when you go further into the different degrees you have fewer people going to school in person. You can also see that once you get the bachelor's degree, you have more people starting to do it all online or half online and half in person rather than doing it fully in person. I wonder if these people have become lazy, are more busy with things like work, or do not enjoy leaving their house. This relates to our community because even though we show up to school every day and sit at a desk, a good amount of our work is now online and dealing with the computer. In classes like math or science, we do a lot of work on paper, but all of our work is done on the computer when it comes to English.

I notice that the amount of in person workers increases as the education level goes down.

I wonder if this is true because older businesses that require a full education are more capable of going online because of the type of work, versus jobs available to those with a high school education who can easily get in person jobs such as working in restaurants, fast food places, or construction.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community by looking at the amount of graduates who were unable to get a higher education due to COVID-19, leading many of them to work in construction, refineries, or go to the military.
"Educational rank and its relation to Coronavirus."

1. This graph took me back to the year 2020 when most of world was in lock-down quaranteen. I can infer from this graph that after the virus outbreak, a larger percentage of people still worked in person. Although an abundant amount of people went back to in-person jobs, a percentage of people decided that working a hybrid or remote status was the way to go. 
2. I began to wonder after analyzing this graph if starting to work remote was more benefical for some people. I wondered if job opportunities were more available due to the fact that a person can perform a duty from the convienence of their own home rather than travel away to earn their paycheck. I also thought about people with hybrid jobs and how the flexibility of working both in ther office and in their own home can help them perform their job at a higher rate. 
3. I felt a connection between this graph and my community because after the pandemic, numerous companies and businesses in my community never went back to being in person and remained or became strictly remote. 
4. Headline: The Dominace of Remote Occupations VS. In-Person Occupations
