raw_comment:
1. One thing that I notice is that a lot of the workers either went to high school or did not even graduate from high school. The graph declines a good amount for some college, but almost stays the same for bachelor's degree. One you get to a Graduate degree, it declines drastically. This can show that some people chose to get their degree and begin working so that they can pay for their debts and needs.
2. I wonder what this graph would have looked like during the pandemic.
3. This relates to me and my community because during the pandemic everyone was doing everything from home. Homework was all online, jobs were online, but as soon as the pandemic was over, everyone went back to in person. Nobody really liked having to do the work from online so everyone was happy to be able to go back in person.
4. "Did the pandemic affect workers in their everyday life?"

Working in a world of semi-normalcy 
I first noticed in this graph that most people in all these fields have returned to in-person work after COVID-19.  What I wonder about after looking at the graph is why the percentage of people who work In person is the highest in the bar of people who only have a high school education or less. This graph relates to me and my community because it shows me that if I want to work fully remotely I would have to have a college education or higher. It also shows how far our community has grown since COVID and how we can work towards going back to a semi-normal society.

raw_comment:
After looking at the graph, I noticed that although most people continue to work in person, there is a gradual shift toward more hybrid and fully remote workers. 

After studying the information, I wonder if the numbers of hybrid and fully remote workers will increase, or if now, since the pandemic is almost over, we will see a resurgence of in-person jobs. 

This chart relates to me because the information it projects relates to my future. As I grow up, the availability of in-person, hybrid, and fully remote jobs will determine where I work and how I work, so it is important that I educate myself. The data depicted also affects my community because the more people that work hybrid or fully remote, the fewer social interactions that occur, and the fewer buildings that need to be constructed to house all of these workers.

raw_comment:
I notice two things mainly:  The first thing being the fact that there is a considerably larger amount of workers that have only graduated high school, compared to the amount of workers with full-blown Graduate degrees.  This can probably be chocked up to the fact that achieving a Graduate degree in any field takes time and dedication, and just working out of high school is much simpler and can usually reap the same rewards.  The second thing I notice is the fact that individuals with college degrees (presumably those who don't have to work in person like blue-collar workers or related careers straight out of high school) have a higher percentage of people who work remotely or in a hybrid manner.  I assume jobs that spawn from collegiate learning most likely offer more opportunity to work with computers, hence the ability to work remotely.

What I mainly wonder is if more people have chosen to take up work just out of high school compared to previous years.  I think such a deduction could be made if we were presented with a graph of similar data from previous years.  I cannot assume, however, that such data would conform to my hypothesis.

How does this relate to my community?  I could apply this same data as an outline to my own graduating class.  It may be possible to assume what percentage of my class will work straight out of high school, continue on to college, or even continue on to high degrees.

"The Rise of Remoteness : In Person Working Takes a Drop in Popularity"

After looking at the graph, I notice that although a significant majority of people continue to work in person, there is a gradual shift toward more hybrid and fully remote workers. 

After studying the information, I wonder if the numbers of hybrid and fully remote workers will increase, or if now, since the pandemic is almost over, we will see a resurgence in person jobs. 

This chart relates to me because the information in projects relates to my future. As I grow up, the availability of in person, hybrid, and fully remote jobs will determine where I work and how I work so it is important to educate myself. The data depicted affects my community because the more people that work hybrid or fully remote, the less social interactions that occur and the fewer buildings that will need to be constructed to house all of these workers. 

Headline: Covid-19's Dramatic Effects on America's Types of Workers.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
This graph is centered around working habits in 2023 since the pandemic. Every category (high school or less, some college, bachelor’s degree, graduate’s degree) has a significantly higher number of in-person workers than any other type of worker. The hybrid type of worker is the smallest within all of the education categories. It appears that about half as many people have a graduate degree than have an education in high school or less.

What do you wonder?
Why is there such a significant difference in the number of fully remote, in-person, and hybrid workers? Did they not have a choice or did they decide to go back? What made that many people decide to go back to work in person?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because the pandemic has impacted the jobs of my parents and many other members of the community. Because of the pandemic, my dad now is able to work hybrid. As a student, I have also had to deal with in-person, fully remote, and hybrid learning, so I have some experience that relates to this graph.

"Post-Pandemic Habits: Is Working In-Person Becoming Infectious?"

raw_comment:
Leah Opdycke
Ms. Wood
AP Lang
18 November 2024
WGOITG
	I noticed that there is still a significantly greater amount of in-person workers than any other type. I also see that workers with Bachelor’s degrees have the most hybrid and remote workers and that workers with high school or less education have the least hybrid and remote workers. 
	I wonder if and how education level directly correlates to whether or not a person works remotely rather than in person. I also wonder why the second greatest number of remote/hybrid workers come from the category of those with graduate degrees. It’s the smallest category, so that means that the ratio of remote/hybrid workers to in-person workers is the closest to 50-50. I wonder why that’s the case. 
	This relates to me and my community because pretty soon I will be looking for a job, so the spread of working remotely may affect me. I may be one of the people who works hybrid or remotely, especially if the trend resulting from the pandemic continues. 
Headline: Spreading Like a Virus: The Expansion of Remote Work Schedules

raw_comment: I can notice that there are many more people who work in person than hybrid or fully remote, not nearly as many people as I expected after the pandemic. I also notice that those who go to college work jobs that are more hybrid and online compared to those with no college education. I wonder what makes college students work more online and hybrid than those who only graduated high school, and why do people with bachelor's degrees specifically have the most online and hybrid jobs. This relates to me and my community because we experienced the pandemic firsthand, and many of the teachers at my school had to switch to online or hybrid teaching strictly, however now they have in-person jobs only. A catchy headline would be "What type of work do different education levels pursue?"

What do you notice?
I noticed that as the education gets higher there tends to be more virtual work. It could be hybrid or completely online, either way there is more of this for higher education.
What do you wonder? 
I wonder why higher education can work more online. I wonder what the advantages and disadvantages of working from home are compared to working in person.
How does this affect you and your community? 
This affects my community because I see people all around me who work from home and I wonder what they had to do to get that? 
Title
Degrees Unlocking Distance Work Opportunities

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I noticed that as the level of education increases, more people seem to be learning virtually or through hybrid models. For example, bachelor’s degrees have a mix of virtual and in-person learning, while high school or less is mostly in-person. 

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why higher levels of education have more virtual or hybrid learning options, while lower levels, like high school, are mostly in-person. Is it because the curriculum for higher education is more adaptable to online formats, or are there other factors at play? I’m also curious about how many people this data is based on and how accurate it is in reflecting broader trends.

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
In my community, there’s been a shift toward more virtual learning after COVID-19, especially in higher education. I see that trend reflected in the graph, where virtual learning is more common for bachelor’s degrees and beyond. Personally, my mom, who has the highest level of education, attends in-person classes, which aligns with the fact that more people with advanced degrees still prefer in-person learning, even though hybrid options exist.

4. Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
“Post-Pandemic Shift: Virtual Learning Dominates Higher Education, While Blue-Collar Jobs Keep it In-Person”

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
I notice that people with only a high school education are more likely to have to work in person compared to people that have a bachelor’s degree. I also noticed that the more education a person obtains, the more likely they are to work hybrid or remote jobs in general (not including graduate degrees). Lastly, I observed that each square on the graph represents 50,000 workers.
What do I wonder?
I wonder if the discrepancy between the amount of remote workers with just a high school diploma compared to a bachelor’s degree is due to the types of jobs. For example, a high school diploma won’t get very high-tech jobs, but a graduate degree may be able to offer higher-tech jobs. I also wonder if more people work remotely when having a bachelor’s degree compared to a graduate degree because of different levels of positions due to the different education levels.
How does this relate to you and your community?	
This relates to me because my dream job is to become a data scientist. Data scientists are one of the most common remote jobs that require a bachelor’s degree. Since I plan on becoming a data scientist someday, it is interesting to see the percentage of people with a bachelor’s degree or graduate degree working remotely or hybrid.
“Working Remote: How Education Shapes Our Work”

Education controls how we work.

It's also interesting how there is a low percentage on people who have graduate degree and an extremely high percentage of people who have a high school education or less. 
3. This relates to me and my community because I, aswell as my friends are about to go to college soon and start out our lives. It is important to know what types of jobs we can receive based on our education. 
4.  Headline: How your education can reflect your future.

1. I noticed that those who graduated High School are those with the largest population on the graph. Of people working remotely and hybrid, the people who received their Bachelor's and Graduate Degrees work remotely the most. As expected people who didn't finish high school, and did not finish college work in person the most. 
2. I wonder why there is a major decline in those who aim to receive a Graduate Degree and why there's a large population of high school graduates, non-high school graduates, and non-college graduates. 
3. This graph relates to me and my community because I am a high school senior who is choosing to go to college, this major decision will change my course in life and not just mine but many of my fellow classmates as well who may choose to further their education or not. 
4. Education and its impact on your work environment.

I notice that the less education you have the more likely you are to have an In-person job. 

I wonder if people who choose to get an even higher education, like a bachelor's degree, do so because they have more chances of having a hybrid or fully remote job. 

This affects me and my community because many people in Perth Amboy are forced to work instead of having the option of getting a degree or a bachelor's because they need to support their families.

raw_comment:
There is a definite increase in the percentages of hybrid or remote workers within the confines of higher education. With High-school graduates that lack further education the most "in-person" workers. Whereas college degrees seem to allow a higher number of options as far as career choice goes. This illustration holds accountable the lacking of education as a main factor for diverse career choice. If I could relate this visual to my own community I would state that education on a national scale is important to support higher learning and the betterment of society. However, what education has become (which Is a discriminant conduit of success) limiting those without "education" to become not as perhaps "successful" or have a "diverse career choice"  as someone with a graduate degree. Which goes against the purpose of education; to inspire positive change.
If I could name this graph, I would respectively quote my late grandfather, "That's why you go to college!"

The graph's trend shows that people with higher education levels, such as bachelor's or graduate degrees, are more likely to work in hybrid or fully remote settings, while those with less education tend to work in person. A fitting headline for the graph would be: "Where Do You Work: In-Person, Hybrid, or Fully Remote?"

raw_comment: * What stood out to me is that independent of degree, in person workers dominate the workforce. However what stood out to me, is that those with a bachelors degree work more hybrid numerically, but proportionally those with a graduate degree have more hybrid workers and less workers overall. This stands out to me because those with the highest level degree are those that work the least overall. This is interesting because it would be expected to be the opposite, but can be explained by those working blue collar jobs having to work multiple different professions and shifts since they make less on average, than those that already reached a certain level of success and are able to make the most of their leisurely time as well. raw_comment: The chart represents the number of people working online, mixed and offline, based online.  The chart separates people by their background, for the next analysis the relative number of groups will be mentioned not absolute. Despite the graph's description mentioning COVID-19, we do not get any comparison of before and after COVID-19 jobs spread. The amount of mixed stays is between 75-100% of the fully remote, the mixed percentage also increases with education level. Overall the question that this chart raises is: Why do people who have lower education levels have more percentage working in person; Why do people tend to work remotely; What is the influence of COVID-19 on this? So they had to go online and not in person finding ways to work the job from home or a little bit of both. Now once the pandemic rolled over, and people started going back to offices still some noticed that they could work just as good or maybe better from home so there was no real reason to go back into the office if it was suitable for them. Now with this said I would say it relates because within my family, and community. One of my family members job was fully in person and around the country before but now is basically fully remote which I think they like more.

raw_comment: One interesting thing I have noticed about this graphic is the fact that interestingly, Bachelor’s Degree students are the individuals who take the most advantage of online and hybrid commuting options. This fact is fascinating to me in particular because being that I am currently in high-school, and especially due to my generation’s adept use of technology and social platforms, I had assumed wrongly that students between the grades of 7-12 would be the most frequent users of online commuting services/resources. This leads me to wonder, what about a bachelor’s program as well as a student’s life at that age leads to more of an interest in online and hybrid programs? And what is leading to the very minimal difference in online commuting between a bachelor’s degree program and a graduate degree program? This relates to me especially due to the fact that I will soon be going to college, as such it is important for me to better understand the origin of these statistics furthermore so that I may be able to make more well-educated decisions as to what course options suit me best for the caree that I am pursuing. I also believe that this is important information for both junior and senior student’s to acknowledge in their educational journies regardless of their career choice. In conclusion, now having given my perspective on this graphic, I would bistowe the title “America’s Rise in Telecommuting; School Edition.”

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph illustrates the number of students attending in-person, hybrid, or fully remote classes across various educational levels, including high school, college, graduate programs, and certificate courses. In every category, there are more in-person students compared to the other formats. This suggests that many individuals prefer attending school or college in person rather than working from home. 

I wonder why people choose to participate in in-person classes rather than studying remotely, where they can complete their schoolwork or college assignments from home. This observation resonates with my community, where many individuals prefer engaging in activities in person, such as attending parades or festivals, rather than experiencing them virtually. 

A catchy headline for this topic might be “In-Person vs. Hybrid Learning.”
